Animal cells lyse in hypotonic and crenate in hypertonic solutions; plant cells become turgid or plasmolyze because a wall resists. `0.9%` NaCl is isotonic to human plasma, which is exactly why it is the default intravenous fluid. Osmosis and all facilitated diffusion are passive; only pumps and bulk transport cost ATP.

scenarios.title: Problem set: reading a pedigree and running the numbers
scenarios.intro: Your genetics problem set gives a four-generation pedigree for a disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness beginning in early childhood. Squares are males, circles females, filled symbols affected. Every affected individual in the chart is male. Two unaffected couples have affected sons. No affected father has an affected son. You are asked to determine the inheritance pattern and then calculate risks.

steps.prompt: First question: unaffected parents in generation II have an affected son. What does that single fact rule out?

choices.text: It rules out a dominant pattern, because a dominant allele would have to be present in a parent to appear in a child
choices.feedback: Correct, and this is the first move in every pedigree problem. Unaffected parents with an affected child means the allele was carried silently, which is the definition of recessive.

choices.text: It rules out a recessive pattern, since recessive traits skip no generations
choices.feedback: Backwards. Recessive traits are precisely the ones that skip generations, because heterozygous carriers show nothing.

choices.text: It rules out sex linkage
choices.feedback: It does not. Sex linkage is about which chromosome carries the gene; dominance is a separate question answered first.

steps.prompt: Second question: every affected individual is male, and no affected father passes the trait to a son. Autosomal recessive or X-linked recessive, and why?

choices.text: X-linked recessive, because males are hemizygous for X genes and fathers give sons only a Y
choices.feedback: Exactly right, and both halves of the reasoning matter. Male predominance points at the X; absence of father-to-son transmission confirms it, since sons get the father's Y.

choices.text: Autosomal recessive, because the trait skips generations
choices.feedback: Skipping generations fits any recessive trait, so it does not distinguish the two. The strong male bias and the transmission pattern do.

choices.text: Y-linked, because only males are affected
choices.feedback: Y-linked traits pass from every affected father to every son with no exceptions. The pedigree explicitly shows no father-to-son transmission, which excludes this.

steps.prompt: Third question: a woman in generation III is the daughter of a carrier mother and an unaffected father. She marries an unaffected man. What is the probability that a given son of hers is affected?

choices.text: 1/4, because she has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier and each son of a carrier has a 1/2 chance
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the multiplication rule for independent events: `1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4`. Ignoring her own carrier probability is the most common error on this item type.

choices.text: 1/2, because carrier mothers pass the allele to half their sons
choices.feedback: That is the conditional answer if she is known to be a carrier. Here her carrier status is itself only 1/2 likely, so the unconditional risk is halved again.

choices.text: 0, because her father was unaffected
choices.feedback: Her father is irrelevant to an X-linked allele she could inherit from her carrier mother. Fathers contribute a Y to sons and an unaffected X to daughters.

steps.prompt: Fourth question: the problem set switches to an autosomal dihybrid cross. Two parents are both `AaBb`, genes on separate chromosomes. What fraction of offspring are `aabb`, and what is the efficient way to get there?

choices.text: 1/16, found by multiplying the two independent monohybrid probabilities `1/4 x 1/4`
choices.feedback: Right, and the method matters more than the number. Treat a dihybrid as two monohybrids and multiply; a 16-cell Punnett square gives the same answer far more slowly.

choices.text: 1/16, found by drawing out the full 16-box Punnett square and counting
choices.feedback: The answer is right and the method works, but on a timed exam it is slow and error-prone. The probability shortcut scales to three and four genes where a grid does not.

choices.text: 1/8, because there are eight possible gamete combinations
choices.feedback: There are four gamete types per parent, not eight, and the combination of interest is a single cell out of sixteen. Count gametes carefully before dividing.

steps.prompt: Last question: in a different family, a couple who both show a dominant phenotype produce a child with the recessive phenotype. The instructor asks what the parents' genotypes must be and whether a test cross would have predicted this.

choices.text: Both parents are heterozygous, and a test cross to a homozygous recessive would have revealed it by producing recessive offspring
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. An affected recessive child proves each parent carried one recessive allele, and a test cross is exactly the tool for exposing a hidden recessive allele.

choices.text: One parent is homozygous dominant and the other heterozygous
choices.feedback: Impossible. A homozygous dominant parent gives every child at least one dominant allele, so no child could show the recessive phenotype.

choices.text: Both parents are heterozygous, but no cross could have predicted the outcome
choices.feedback: The genotypes are right but the second half is wrong. A test cross to a homozygous recessive individual is designed precisely to expose heterozygosity.

scenarios.debrief: Two habits carry most genetics points. First, read a pedigree in a fixed order: dominant or recessive, then autosomal or sex-linked. Unaffected parents with an affected child means recessive; heavy male predominance with no father-to-son transmission means X-linked. Second, convert every cross into independent probabilities and multiply, rather than drawing grids. Remember to include upstream uncertainty, such as a parent's own 1/2 chance of being a carrier, before multiplying downstream. And remember that each pregnancy is an independent event: a family with three affected children still faces the same per-pregnancy risk on the fourth.
